flawed_step: The claim that normality passes to arbitrary subspaces; it only passes to closed subspaces in general.
counterexample: Tychonoff plank P=[0,ω1]×[0,ω] (order topologies) is compact Hausdorff, hence normal (T1+T4). Deleted plank T=P\{(ω1,ω)}. A={ω1}×[0,ω) and B=[0,ω1)×{ω} are disjoint and closed in T (their closures in P add only the removed corner point). If U⊇A, V⊇B are open in T: for each n pick αn<ω1 with (αn,ω1]×{n}⊆U; α=sup αn<ω1; β=α+1. Then (β,ω)∈B, so V contains (γ,β]×(m,ω] for some γ<β, m<ω, which contains (β,m+1)∈U. So U∩V≠∅, and T is not normal.
assessment_summary: Counterexample: the deleted Tychonoff plank, a subspace of the compact Hausdorff (hence normal) plank [0,ω1]×[0,ω]. In it, the sets {ω1}×[0,ω) and [0,ω1)×{ω} are disjoint and closed but cannot be separated, because the ordinal ω1 cannot be reached by a countable sequence of countable ordinals. So normality is not hereditary.
